newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: LITHUANIA BROKERS WANT STEPS TO BOOST BOURSE.
newsitem.headline: LITHUANIA BROKERS WANT STEPS TO BOOST BOURSE.

text.p: The head of Lithuania's brokers association said on Thursday he wanted measures to boost trade on the country's struggling stock market, including an overhaul of the trading system to allow a continuous market.
National Brokers Association chief Romas Matiukas said the stock exchange should also lower transaction fees and make better use of block trading to inject liquidity into the market.

Matiukas said changing the trading system at the bourse was one of the association's priorities and that a short-term solution would be to allow block trading to develop as much as possible towards continuous trading.
"We want to develop the block market into a continuous market as far as it is possible," Matiukas said. "But there is a need for technical and organisational support."

Prices on the central market are set once daily. Matiukas said modifying the central market just to allow two or three fixings a day would be expensive and that a new trading system was necessary if the bourse was to achieve continuous trading.
"We can live for some time reforming the block trades market but in the future it will be impossible to live without a new system," Matiukas said.

He added that the process of improving block trading has already started, with the removal of margins of price fluctuations in May. The next steps are the computerisation of transactions and transparency for block trades.
"A drawback of the stock exchange is the large fees, commissions to the stock exchange," he added.
Transaction fees are currently 0.25 percent for buyer and seller on non-official list shares, Matiukas said.
"So the cost of every transaction is really 0.50 percent," Matiukas said. "It makes it very costly for investors who want to speculate on the market and therefore there is no liquidity."
The commission for official list shares is 0.15 percent.
Matiukas said the brokers association has not decided what it would like the fees to be changed to.
Brokers recently dealt with a spate of suspensions of their favourite shares for formalities including shareholders meetings, a company reorganisation and share assimilations.
Brokers say the suspensions worsen the liquidity problem on the sleepy bourse by keeping popular shares inactive.

The brokers association is pushing for the securities commission to reduce the suspensions so they would take place only when trading would be technically impossible -- like when new share issues are joining the shares.
Matiukas expects the securities commission to decide on changes to rules on suspensions in June.

To minimise suspensions, Matiukas said parliament must change the law on stock companies to institute recording days for deciding shareholder lists for payments of dividends, shareholder meetings, bonus issues and rights issues.
"When recording days are introduced, it will not be necessary to stop trading a week before shareholders meetings," Matiukas said.
Matiukas said parliament may decide on the changes to company law at the end of June.
